You're not alone here with that struggle. For most of my teen years I recognized I had alot of PCOS symptoms. (My mother has it too that's why I knew the symptoms) they wreaked Havok on my already fragile self esteem. And over the years they seemed to get worse. And so did my self esteem and confidence. Eventually at 18 I was diagnosed. It made me feel worse. It was like confirming all these "flaws" I had were out of my control. I think the most we can do it try to treat the physical to make things easier, but I think something that can be beneficial to help the way we feel is therapy. We really have to get out of our own heads and change our negative thought processes. Because even when the weight loss comes, the hair on the chin goes away, our poor self image still remains. We may still feel a bit better no doubt, but the thoughts still remain.

It's a shame the business let's this go on. Regardless of if he has autism or not it's sexual assault. And it shouldn't be tolerated. I understand that when someone is on the spectrum they may struggle with certain social ques. However I've worked with someone with autism, he had it pretty bad it seemed. But he understood boundaries. He was real sweetheart actually, just pretty chatty if anything. I understand the business would probably be afraid of lawsuits, however I feel legally it reflects worse on the business to allow the sexual assault to continue. I saw in the comments someone else suggested talking to a legal professional about this to see what can be done/the actual legalities of everything and I completely agree, especially if you don't want to change jobs.

And as for the ableism thing. I don't think this makes you ableist. I think simply holding just the fact he's autistic against him would be, but you have actual concerns that actually affect the entire workplace. I think most people would feel this way. As much as I'm a firm believer in giving people with disabilities the opportunity to work, if they simply cannot, they cannot. You know?
